Power v Giants: opposition report and game plan

Performance analysis, prepared for the senior coach. Source: the season tracking database (244 games: the Giants' and the Power's 112 games each against 28 common opponents, plus 20 head-to-heads), the league position rating tool, and the league match engine. Every number below comes from that data. The working notebook (notebook.md) and scripts (work/) hold the detail.

The short version

  1. The Giants kick, mark and kick again, and almost never handball (0.8 handballs a game; 98% of their marks are kicked straight away, 0.4 s after the mark). Up front they hold two forwards out very wide and one central target, and feed the wide men into the middle. High confidence
  2. Without the ball they sit off and intercept. They put less pressure on the ball carrier than anyone (0.55 in their back 50, against 1.35 from the league against them) and read the kick: their three defenders intercept-marked 13.8% of the Power's kicks in our 20 meetings (8.5% for other clubs). Intercept marks gave them 27% of their points against us. High confidence
  3. Their kicking breaks down under pressure. In their back third against us they kept 80% of kicks unpressured and 62% under pressure. Because they never handball, they have no outlet. Our wins came with more pressure (correlation with our margin r = +0.52) and fewer Giants intercepts (2.6 a game in wins, 3.9 in losses). Medium-high confidence
  4. They run themselves into the ground. Their players spend 55-59% of the time above sprint pace (Power 34-36%). By the second minute their midfielders are at about a quarter of full energy and their forwards at about a third. We win 58% of contested ground balls against them. Medium-high confidence
  5. We play into their hands in two ways. (a) Our defenders punch the ball away even when no Giant is there: 3.2 uncontested spoils a game. (b) We kick long into the corridor from set plays: 23% of those are intercepted. Both are easy to fix. Medium-high confidence

Game plan in one line: press their kicker with our (fresh) forwards, mark the ball when alone, stop feeding their interceptors with set-play kicks into the corridor and short chips, and keep the ball on the ground where their tired midfield loses. We are already modest favourites: 11 wins, 1 draw, 8 losses, +4.0 points a game. The aim is to remove the games we lose.

1. Recommendations: how the Power should play the Giants

  1. Press the Giants' kicker, especially in their back half, and use the forwards to do it. Medium-high confidence
    What to change: today only our midfielders tackle: all 212 of our tackles this season (182 against others, 30 against the Giants) were by m1/m2, and our forwards sprint only 16% of the time. Give the nearest forward (or midfielder) the job of closing the Giants' ball carrier during their 0.4 s gather. This matters most on their back-third kicks, about 6 a game of which are currently unpressured.
    Why the data says it works: Giants kick retention falls from 70% unpressured to 55% under heavy pressure (44% against us). Our own retention does not fall, because we handball. The league rating tool, applied to 163 real head-to-head frames, values putting our nearest player on their carrier at +1.4 percentage points of "Power scores the next goal" each time (positive in 90% of cases). That is after charging for the man left free. In the match engine, one extra presser on 91 real Giants kicks cut their retention from 52.6% to 48.5%, and our win-backs rose from 30% to 35%. Our forwards have the energy budget: estimated 0.80 against the Giants' defenders' 0.60. And a chain that starts in our forward 35 is worth 1.7-2.2 points.
    Risk: a pressing forward leaves a Giants defender free. The rating test already includes that cost, and the Giants' back-half chains are their least productive (0.12 points per chain).
  2. Mark it when you are alone. Spoil only when a Giant is there. Medium-high confidence
    What to change: half of our spoils against the Giants are uncontested (3.2 a game). A spoil gives back a loose ball we regain 85% of the time; a mark is a protected set play we keep about 95% of the time.
    Why: on the 65 real uncontested head-to-head spoils, the rating tool scores "our defender holding the ball" +5.1 pp above the loose ball that actually followed (95% of cases positive). Defenders are strong marks by the league's own player profile. When a Giant is there, keep spoiling to ground: we win 58% of contested ground balls against them.
  3. Stop feeding their interceptors: no long set-play kicks into the corridor, and no short chips. Medium confidence
    What to change: from a mark, either play on quickly (handball or run), or kick only to a forward who has broken clear (no Giant within ~10 m), usually 22-35 m away. Drop the 15-22 m chip (about 30% of our general-play kicks).
    Why: the Giants intercept 23% of our set-play kicks and 21% of our unpressured kicks (6% when we kick under pressure). Their defenders set up goal-side while our kicker takes his time. In the engine, our kicks to a teammate with no Giant within 10 m were kept 73% of the time, against 54-59% when a Giant was within 10 m. A free forward 22-40 m away was available in 53% of situations. Across the whole season, our sub-22 m kicks start chains worth 0.52 points (from the defensive midfield), against 1.03-1.49 for longer kicks.
    How: our forwards are almost static (16% sprint). Timed leads into space are what create the free target. That is my inference, not directly measured.
  4. Make their midfield run, and keep the ball low. Medium confidence
    Why: the Giants' midfielders sit at an estimated 0.25 energy from the second minute (about 62% of top pace); ours at 0.37-0.39. When two players reach a loose ball at similar distance with an energy gap above 0.2, the fresher one wins 58% (1,686 cases). The Giants score least in the third minute against us (1.75 points a game). We score 4.0 points a game in each of minutes 2 and 3 against them (4.8 in minute 3 against others). Avoid floating kicks to contests where their defenders mark. Ground-ball contests and quick handball chains suit us.
  5. Defend the Giants' forward pattern: f1/f3 wide into f2 central. Medium confidence
    Why: 43% of their f1's kicks and 38% of their f3's go to the central f2, and f2 kicks out to the wide men 60% of the time. Our d2 is the key player: stay goal-side of their f2 and let the wide feed come. Against us, Giants kicks from their forward midfield (70-105 m) are already kept only 49% of the time, and their goal conversion is poor (29% in general, 31% against us). Keep contesting the shooter: 36% of their shots come under heavy pressure.
  6. Centre bounces: keep doing what we do. High confidence
    The m1 v m1 bounce is a coin flip with identical players (we win 55% against them). Energy makes no difference (r = 0.02). Our clearance after winning it is the best part of our game against them: kept 78% of the time, and we score next 65% of the time. Do not change it.

2. How the Giants play

With the ball

Mean landing width |y|16.4 m11.0 m15.6 m
Kicks retained62%64%66%
Shots, goal %5.8 a game, 29%5.8, 39%7.1, 33%
  • Midfield (m1, m2): m1 takes every centre bounce; both follow the ball at about 15-17 m. They are the main kickers (27% of kicks) and kick forward to the three forwards (52% of m1 kicks). They never handball, and they sprint 66-70% of the time.
  • Forwards: f2 stays in the central corridor (|y| 2-6 m). f1 and f3 hold very wide (|y| ≈ 30 m when the ball is in the Giants' back half, ≈ 20 m in their front third). Their football runs wide → centre → wide (Figure 3). They sprint 62% of the time (Power forwards 16%).
  • Defenders: d2 central, d1/d3 at 12-17 m width. They match up loosely, about 11 m from their direct opponent (zone mirroring, not tight man-on-man). They kick to f1/f2, retain 65%, and take 73% of their short kick-ins (27 m) cleanly.

Without the ball

  • They sit off and protect space. Pressure on the opposition carrier (league scale 0-2): Giants 0.78 overall and 0.55 in their own back 50. The league applies 1.11 against them and 1.35 in that zone. Their defensive line is ordinary, not high. I checked this because the first read suggested a high line; that read was wrong.
  • They intercept-mark rather than spoil. 2.2 intercept marks a game against others and 3.15 against us (the Power: 0.18). They spoil only 2.3 times a game, and 99% of those are contested. Their defenders take 49 of their 63 intercept marks against us.
  • They tackle across all lines (5.4 a game: mids 40%, defenders 34%, forwards 26%).

Stoppages and transition

  • Centre bounces are 50/50 (Giants 52% v others, 45% v us). After winning one, the Giants clear 30 m and keep it 57% of the time against others (67% against us). After losing one they concede the next score 60% of the time, and 39% within 20 seconds.
  • Kick-ins: taken by a defender or midfielder, short (27 m) and towards the corridor; kept 73% of the time (79% against us).
  • Transition: against other clubs, 45% of their points come from chains that start in their forward 35 (forward-half turnovers, 2.2 points per chain). Against us that falls to 25%, and intercept marks take over (27%).

4. How the Power play now, and why the head-to-heads go each way

Our style has been stable all season (handballs 8.6 a game in both halves of the season; tackles 1.9 and 1.3). In short:

  • Narrow and possession-based: mids at |y| 6-8 m, forwards at |y| 14 m. 8.6 handballs a game (retained 82%). We play on from 42% of marks. We kick down the corridor (53% of kicks land within 10 m of the centre line).
  • Static forwards, fresh legs: our forwards sprint 16% of the time and hold ~0.8 energy all game. They lead little.
  • Defence by spoiling: 5.3 spoils a game (6.5 against the Giants), 43-50% of them with no opponent there. We almost never intercept-mark (0.18 a game).
  • Only the midfielders tackle (all 182 tackles this season). Pressure on the carrier is low against others (0.66) but higher against the Giants (1.12).
  • Strengths: centre clearances (kept 78% against the Giants), finishing (39% goals), and scoring from deep: chains starting in our back 35 / defensive midfield are worth 0.34 / 0.78 points (the Giants' equivalents: 0.12 / 0.41).

Why the Giants beat us: they intercept our kicks and turn them into scores, and on those days we also kick badly at goal. Why we beat them: we press their kicker, they turn it over, and we win the ground ball. Twenty games is a small sample: the correlations (pressure +0.52, Giants intercepts −0.42, Giants retention −0.52) point the same way as the larger season-wide evidence, but on their own they would be weak.

5. Testing the ideas

Three kinds of test were run. All of them use real head-to-head positions.

  • League position rating tool (tools/rate_position.py, used unmodified). It was first checked against the database's own ratings: r = 0.96 held ball, 0.89 loose, 0.78 in flight. Then real frames were edited one change at a time and re-rated.
  • League match engine (_engine): real frames loaded into the physics, with the disposal replayed 12-20 times under each option. Off-ball players use the same neutral contest rule for both sides.
  • Observational comparisons within the season data, holding the zone of the ground fixed.
IdeaResultVerdict

Mark, don't spoil, when aloneRating +5.1 pp per instance (n = 65); regain 85% (spoil) v ~95% (mark)Recommended
Kick to a free forward 22-35 m away; drop the short chipEngine: 73% (free) v 54-59% (Giant within 10 m); short kicks start chains worth half as muchRecommended
Kick wide rather than down the corridorIntercepts lower wide (3% v 16%) but small sample (65 wide kicks); the rating tool slightly prefers central; value change flatNot recommended: inconclusive

6. What I could not establish, and how far to trust this

  • Coaching instructions are not in the data. Everything about "what the Giants are told" is inferred from behaviour. The behaviour itself is very consistent across 132 games.
  • Energy is estimated, not measured. I rebuilt it from tracking speeds using the league's published energy rule. The direction (the Giants sprint far more and are much more tired) rests on directly measured sprint time and top speeds. The exact levels (e.g. 0.25) are approximate.
  • The tests are partial models. The rating tool does not know about set-play protection and is not very sensitive to where a kick lands. The engine tests move only the ball carrier, the presser and nearby contesters: off-ball players do not lead or re-position. So the absolute retention rates in the simulations are lower than in real matches (our actual kicks: 47% simulated v 65% real). Only the comparisons between options are meaningful.
  • Opponent reaction is unknown. If we press, the Giants may start to handball. They already handball 2.0 a game against us, against 0.8 against others, so they do adapt a little. If our forwards press, the Giants' defenders get more space behind them.
  • Small head-to-head sample. 20 games. Margins swing from Giants +12 to Power +18, and goal accuracy alone moves results a lot. Treat head-to-head-only findings as supporting evidence.
  • Not quantified: the effect of leads by our forwards (recommended on reasoning, not measured); the scoreboard effect of each change in points. I give per-instance effects and how often each situation occurs, not a points forecast.

Method notes. All positions are converted to each club's frame (attacking left to right, a 180° rotation for away games). Possession chains are runs of control by one club. Pressure uses the league formula (sum of exp(−(d/5)²), capped at 2). "League v Giants" means the 28 common opponents in their games against the Giants. Scripts: work/*.py; figures: fig/; notebook: notebook.md.
